procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 27.06.2007 of the High Court of Karnataka at Bangalore in Cr. A. No. 1642 of 2005.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court partly allowed the appeal (Cr. A. No. 1642 of 2005). It acquitted the appellant's father of all charges/offences. It maintained the appellant's conviction under Sections 498-A I.P.C. and 306 I.P.C., but acquitted the appellant for other offences.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court (Criminal Appeal No. 1606 of 2009). The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision regarding the appellant's conviction under Sections 498-A I.P.C. and 306 I.P.C.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellant under Sections 498-A and 306 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.) was justified.

facts: The appellant's wife committed suicide within four months of their marriage.
The prosecution alleged that the suicide was a result of cruelty and dowry harassment, specifically because the appellant was having an illicit relationship with another woman.
The appellant had previously admitted before a Panchayat that he was living with another woman and had signed an agreement promising to end the relationship and live with his wife.
The trial court and the High Court had both convicted the appellant under Sections 498-A and 306 of the I.P.C.
law: The issue centered on Sections 498-A (cruelty by husband or his relatives) and 306 (abetment of suicide) of the Indian Penal Code.

The appellant's counsel argued that a conviction for abetment of suicide under Section 306 requires 'mens rea' (a guilty mind) and a direct act that leads the person to commit suicide, which they claimed was absent in this case.
application: The Court found that the prosecution had provided sufficient evidence to uphold the conviction.
It gave significant weight to a documentary evidence, an agreement from a Panchayat, in which the appellant admitted to his illicit affair.

The Court also relied on the consistent testimony of multiple prosecution witnesses (PW-1, PW-6, PW-10, and PW-22) who stated that the appellant continued his illicit relationship even after the Panchayat agreement.
The Court reasoned that the appellant's continued illicit relationship would have "definitely created the psychological imbalance to the deceased."

It concluded that this psychological imbalance, caused by the appellant's conduct, directly led the victim to take the extreme step of committing suicide, thus fulfilling the requirements for abetment under Section 306 I.P.C.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had rightly maintained the conviction of the appellant under Sections 498-A and 306 I.P.C., and therefore, the conviction was justified.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellant under Sections 498-A and 306 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.) was justified.
appellant_arguments: The appellant, the accused-husband, challenged the conviction under Sections 498-A and 306 of the I.P.C., arguing it was not justified.
respondent_arguments: The respondent-State argued in favor of upholding the conviction, contending that the High Court had rightly maintained the conviction of the appellant under Sections 498-A and 306 of the I.P.C.

cases.case_name: Randhir Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: Abetment involves a mental process of instigating a person or in any manner aiding that person in doing of the thing.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction under Sections 498-A and 306 of the Indian Penal Code can be upheld when it is justified by the specific evidence presented in the case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's decision to maintain the conviction of the appellant under Sections 498-A and 306 of the Indian Penal Code was correct, basing its own conclusion on the evidence on record and a specific document, the 'Agreement dated 22nd June, 2002'.
legal_tests_applied: Abetment involves a mental process of instigating a person or in any manner aiding that person in doing of the thing. Courts should carefully assess the facts of each case before deciding whether the cruelty meted out to the victim which induces her to commit suicide.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that there was no mens rea or a direct act leading to the suicide was implicitly rejected, as the court found the conviction was justified based on the evidence and an 'Agreement dated 22nd June, 2002'.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld because the court agreed with the High Court's assessment, concluding that the conviction was rightly maintained based upon the evidence and the 'Agreement dated 22nd June, 2002'.
